extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, examiners, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for construing the scope of patent claims and for filing and effect of disclaimers, including how specification, prosecution history, amendments, and patentee conduct affect claim scope and enforcement rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims measure the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims measure the invention. They may be explained and illustrated by the description. They cannot be enlarged by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define the scope; the specification can clarify but not broaden claim scope beyond the plain import of the claim language (citing Continental Paper Bag Co. v. Eastern Paper Bag Co. and related authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit claim construction to plain import of claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust to construe a claim in a manner different from the plain import of its terms; the claim is a statutory requirement to define precisely what is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should avoid reading into claims elements not present and should not alter the claim to include something more or different than its words express.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import dispensable elements to avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim will not be narrowed by importing into it, by construction, any dispensable element, in order to enable an infringer to escape the consequences of his infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not be artificially narrowed by reading in nonessential/speculative elements from the specification just to avoid finding infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of failure to put invention to practical use
rubrics_metrics.description: When no practical use has been made of the patent the claims will be narrowly construed, the reason being that the patent lacks support from public acquiescence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, a practical success constituting a distinct advance in the art warrants a liberal construction of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings in the Patent Office can prevent narrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims will not be narrowed where the proceedings in the Patent Office clearly show that the inventor intended to claim and the Patent Office intended to grant the broader monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporaneous prosecution history showing intent to obtain broader claims militates against judicial narrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification may illustrate but not enlarge claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The description may explain and illustrate the claim but cannot be used to enlarge the claim beyond its terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions of particular devices or arrangements cannot be treated as limiting absent clear intent; illustrations serve to explain but not to broaden the statutory claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit description of alternatives can affect construction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee explicitly states that there might be alternatives for the device described, courts have given broader construction than if no alternatives were mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A declaration in the specification that alternatives are possible may support a broader claim interpretation than a specification that appears to fix a single arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode disclosure does not necessarily limit claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: While statutory provision requires disclosure of the best mode, it is not clear that this requirement affects the scope of the claims; inventor may state the best mode but not be confined to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee must disclose best mode but may not be confined to only that disclosed mode; patents would be of little worth if so confined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims cannot be construed to cover incidental or recommended processes
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim for a process, substantially as described, cannot be construed to cover an incidental process set forth in the description but merely recommended there, instead of being required or essential to the principal process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended or preferable steps in the specification do not expand the scope of a process claim unless the claim itself includes them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferable language in specification does not restrict claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee of a manufacture is not restricted to a construction which he describes in the specification merely as 'preferable,' unless specifically limited by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements of preference in the spec are insufficient to limit claim scope absent express claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims cannot be altered by construction to cover more or fewer elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim clearly covers a combination of certain elements, it cannot, by construction, be altered to cover more elements so as to be valid, or to cover fewer elements and thus be rendered more likely to be infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not rewrite claims to change the elements covered; claimed combinations stand as written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot read in elements that are not equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim cannot be construed to cover other elements in place of some that may be omitted, unless those omitted elements are equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacement of claim elements by non-equivalents through construction is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's acts and conduct may limit claim (estoppel/laches)
rubrics_metrics.description: The acts and conduct of the owner of a patent (e.g., long-standing constructions placed on a claim with knowledge of noninfringing sales) may give a construction to a claim which will avoid infringement; this may be placed on laches or estoppel grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long acquiescence or conduct that indicates a narrow construction can preclude later assertion of a broader scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous intention and prosecution history admissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent may be construed in the light of the contemporaneous intention of the inventor and of the Patent Office; recourse may be had to the files of the application papers to see what changes were made while the application was pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution history and file wrapper are relevant to ascertain scope, though limits apply (see rules about amendments, estoppel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening changes in prosecution cannot be construed away to save validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the change made in the Patent Office was a broadening one, it cannot be construed away in order to ascribe validity to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant broadened claims during prosecution and obtained allowance, courts will not later construe them as if the broadening did not occur to avoid invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and amendments made to obtain allowance generally bind patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant who, on rejection, inserted limitations and restrictions into his specification for the purpose of obtaining his patent cannot later claim it shall be construed as if such limitations were not contained in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material modifications made in obedience to PTO requirements are ordinarily treated as limiting; however courts recognize undue narrowing and may lean toward liberality where PTO requirements were unwarranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant not precluded from later claims to improvements not disclosed earlier
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant is not precluded from securing by an amended claim every improvement and combination that he has invented and that is not disclosed by the references on which the original claim was rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments adding true new inventions not previously disclosed may be allowable; context of prosecution matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel by prosecution requires relation to the 'pith and marrow'
rubrics_metrics.description: For proceedings in the Patent Office to operate as an estoppel they must relate to the 'pith and marrow' of an alleged improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only concessions or amendments touching the essential core of the claimed invention will create an estoppel; incidental or phraseology-driven amendments will not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidental amendments for phraseology do not limit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely incidental amendments, not made in pursuance of references or real reasons given by the Patent Office, but in deference to PTO preferences for particular phraseology, will not be construed to limit claims so as to make them narrower than the inventions they were designed to cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts avoid giving effect to trivial or stylistic amendments as disclaimers of scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concessions in argument not carried into claims do not limit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Concessions addressed to the Examiner in arguments which are not carried into the claims do not limit the claims as finally allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only what's embodied in claim language and formal amendments ordinarily binds; pure prosecutorial argument lacks the same binding effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawn proposed amendments do not limit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment proposed but subsequently withdrawn cannot be construed to impose a limitation on the claim as issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only successful/entered amendments are relevant to restricting claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws in force at grant control construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws which were in force when any particular patent was granted are the laws according to which it must be construed; a special statute relevant to a particular patent is ingrafted on the general patent statutes and must be harmonized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the statutory and case-law framework in effect at the time of grant when construing older patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction is a question of law; experts limited to terms of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of construction are questions of law for the judge, not of fact for the jury. Judges may avail themselves of experts for the meaning of terms of art or science used in the patent, but expert testimony on construction of the patent as a whole is inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts can explain technical meaning, but ultimate claim interpretation is judicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that patent covers what was in application
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of contrary evidence, the invention covered by a particular letters patent is presumed to be identical with that covered by the application on which those letters patent were granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File history and application content are baseline presumptions for what the patent covers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice: patents are public record but impractical to know all
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons are chargeable with notice of the contents of all letters patent of the United States because they are matters of public record; nevertheless the sheer number and complexity make actual knowledge impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal notice exists, but realistic limitations on human capacity mean infringement inquiries often require expert patent searching and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authorization for disclaimers when patentee claimed too much
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, and without fraudulent or deceptive intention, a patentee has claimed materially more than he was the first inventor of, his patent shall be valid for whatever is justly his own and he may, on payment of fee, make disclaimer of such parts he no longer chooses to claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers remedy overclaiming; they must be in writing, attested, recorded, and state extent of interest. They allow enforcement of the remainder but have procedural consequences (costs, timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and content requirements for disclaimers to recover costs
rubrics_metrics.description: In any suit where judgment is rendered for the plaintiff, no costs shall be recovered unless the proper disclaimer was entered in the Patent Office before commencement of the suit; a patentee who unreasonably neglects or delays to enter a disclaimer is not entitled to maintain such a suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt filing of a proper disclaimer is required to preserve entitlement to costs and to avoid statutory penalties for delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and recording of disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer shall be in writing, attested by one or more witnesses, and recorded in the Patent Office, and shall thereafter be considered part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper execution and recordation are necessary; disclaimers do not affect pending actions except as to unreasonable delay questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes of fact vs. mistakes of law justify disclaimers differently
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors that lead to overclaiming may arise from inadvertence, accident, mistake of fact (e.g., prior art unknown) or mistake of law; statutory scheme contemplates disclaimers primarily where patentee claimed more than he was first to invent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes of fact (novelty-related) often require disclaimer within reasonable time upon discovery; mistakes of law (invention) have different implications discussed in subsequent sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer cannot confine claim to ground not appearing in the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclaimer cannot confine a claim to ground which does not appear in the patent to constitute an invention; even if that ground is narrower than what was originally claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot use a disclaimer to retroactively convert a claim into something that the patent never disclosed as inventive.
